Name: cross_episode_drag_content_not_label
Title: Drag Crosses the Episode Boundary: Failed Prior Episodes in Agent Memory Bias New Episodes Toward Their Errors Through Action Content, Not Outcome Labels, and Abstraction Filters Drag Faster Than Benefit
Short Hypothesis: Contextual drag extends from in-task retries to cross-episode memory: a failed prior episode of the same task type injected as memory biases the agent toward structurally similar errors; the drag is carried by the prior trajectory's action content (flipping or hiding the outcome label leaves it unchanged), successful priors give a smaller symmetric benefit, and LLM abstraction of prior episodes (fold-style outcome summary, then insight) removes the failure drag faster than it removes the success benefit, so the right abstraction level for a store depends on its failure fraction.
Related Work: Contextual Drag (arXiv:2602.04288) shows failed drafts in context bias later generations toward structurally similar errors on eight single-episode reasoning tasks across 11 models, with REVISE and FILTER denoising only partially effective; it does not test cross-episode memory, label manipulation, or abstraction of the failed attempt. The Compliance Trap (arXiv:2607.10608) injects deliberately conflicting memory and traces entry, propagation and recovery, without label dissociation or abstraction levels. Useful Memories Become Faulty (arXiv:2605.12978) traces regression to LLM consolidation and finds an episodic-only control competitive, but does not separate failure content from consolidation error. AdaMEM (arXiv:2606.05684) hybridizes raw long-term and on-the-fly strategy memory; SkillEvolBench (arXiv:2605.24117) finds raw reuse often beats distilled skills; ExpeL, ReMe and Mistake Notebook Learning (arXiv:2512.11485) store failures on purpose as learning signal. None measures whether stored failures transmit their error structure to new episodes, whether the outcome label or the content carries it, or whether abstraction filters the transmission asymmetrically.
Abstract: Condensed state (folds, summaries, insights, raw trajectories) almost always lives inside one episode, so whether carrying it across tasks helps, and whether stale or failed prior episodes induce the contextual drag observed within tasks, is untested. We inject prior episodes of the same ALFWorld task type (different scene and objects) into the context of a new episode and manipulate three things independently: prior outcome (success or failure), the outcome label shown to the agent (true, flipped, hidden), and abstraction level (raw trajectory, fold-style outcome summary of about 100 tokens, one-line ExpeL-style insight), against no-memory, fresh-session and length-matched irrelevant-episode controls. The primary outcome is success; the mechanistic outcome is a drag signature: the rate at which the new episode's first error falls in the same category as the prior episode's error (deterministic ALFWorld error taxonomy: invalid action, wrong receptacle class, wrong object, loop, premature completion) relative to the agent's own no-memory base rate for that category, plus an entry-propagation-recovery trace of when the copied action first appears. Failure priors are drawn both from the same backbone and from a different backbone with a different error distribution, so that copying can be separated from the agent's own attractor failures. The central claims are that drag crosses the episode boundary, that it is label-invariant, that it is asymmetric (failure harm exceeds success benefit), and that abstraction removes failure drag by the summary level while success benefit survives that level. A prospective test then predicts, for stores with failure fractions 0, 0.25 and 0.5, which abstraction level should be carried, and checks it on held-out tasks. Backbones are 8B, 27B-class and 120B MoE open-weight models; paired designs, null replicates and pre-registered margins control noise.
Experiments: Pool construction: run each backbone on the ALFWorld train split to collect success and failure episodes per task type; also collect failure episodes from a second backbone. Failure priors are filtered to those with a clear first error under the taxonomy and truncated to the same step count distribution as success priors. Main design on 500 held-out tasks times two seeds per backbone: memory conditions are a crossing of outcome (success, failure) by label (true, flipped, hidden) by abstraction (raw, summary, insight) with k=1 prior, plus controls (no memory, fresh-session, length-matched irrelevant raw episode from another task type, and raw failure prior from the other backbone). Abstractions are generated once per prior by the same backbone and frozen. Secondary arms: k=3 priors with failure fraction in {0, 1/3, 2/3}; stale priors from scenes where the target object's location differs (a stale-location prior), reported as the mid-stream-shift case. Outcomes per episode: success, first error category, copy indicator (first error category equals the prior's error category), first step at which the agent's action matches the prior's erroneous action, steps, tokens. The prospective store test fixes the abstraction policy predicted by the main design (raw for failure fraction 0, summary for 0.25 and 0.5) and evaluates on a further 300 tasks against the always-raw and always-insight policies.
Baselines and Ablations: Baselines: no memory, fresh-session (same task, no history), length-matched irrelevant raw episode, ExpeL-style insight injection, raw retrieval as in ReMe with k=1. Ablations: prior from same versus different backbone; label position (top versus bottom of the prior); summary generated by the backbone versus by the 120B model; k=1 versus k=3; abstraction token counts reported so that token load is separated from content (the irrelevant raw episode is the token-load control); task-type breakdown; error-taxonomy validation on 200 episodes by two annotators; the stale-location arm.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1 (cross-episode drag): a raw failure prior lowers success by at least 5 points versus no memory on the 8B backbone, and the copy rate exceeds the no-memory base rate for that error category with relative risk at least 1.5, also when the prior comes from the other backbone; if the copy rate matches base rate, drag does not cross the episode boundary. P2 (content not label): success and copy rate under flipped and hidden labels are equivalent to the true-label condition within a pre-registered 3-point margin (TOST); if relabeling a failure as success amplifies harm or hiding the label removes it, the label carries part of the effect and the claim fails in the reported direction. P3 (asymmetry): the raw success benefit is smaller in magnitude than the raw failure harm on every backbone (paired difference, CI excludes 0). P4 (abstraction asymmetry): at the summary level the failure harm is inside the noise band while the success benefit remains above the MDE; if both decay proportionally (ratio of remaining harm to remaining benefit near 1), the asymmetry claim is falsified; if raw success beats summary success by more than the summary-level harm reduction, raw storage wins regardless of failure fraction. P5 (prospective policy): the failure-fraction-conditioned abstraction policy beats always-raw at failure fraction 0.5 and always-insight at failure fraction 0 by more than the MDE on the 300 held-out tasks. P6 (stale prior): a stale-location prior produces a wrong-receptacle copy rate above base rate even when its label is success, showing that staleness acts through content like failure does.
Measurement and Noise Control: All memory conditions are evaluated on the same held-out tasks with the same environment instances and seeds, so contrasts are paired; McNemar on success, exact binomial tests on copy indicators, mixed-effects logistic regression with task random effects and outcome by label by abstraction fixed effects. Null replicates: two independent no-memory runs per backbone give the run-to-run band, which fixes the equivalence margin for P2 and the noise band for P4. MDE: with about 1,000 paired episodes per contrast and discordance near 0.2, roughly 3 to 4 points at alpha 0.05 and power 0.8. Copy rates are compared against the backbone's own no-memory base rate per error category to avoid confounding copying with attractor failures; the different-backbone prior condition is the decisive check. Taxonomy reliability reported as kappa. All margins, the error taxonomy and the abstraction policy rule are pre-registered before the confirmatory run; the prospective policy test is run only after the main design is locked.

Name: gate_reads_style_not_truth
Title: Admission Gates Read Style, Not Truth: A Planted-Record Audit of Write-Time Validation in Agent Experience Memory
Short Hypothesis: Every published write-time admission gate that decides from the candidate record's text alone (LLM-judge validation in ReMe, five-factor admission in A-MAC, goal-conditioned utility tagging in CraniMem, LLM-verified promotion in Atlas) is a classifier of surface form, not of correctness: a wrong record rewritten into the style of previously admitted records is admitted at the same rate as a correct one, so store-level gate precision carries no information about downstream task success; only execution-referenced gates (replay in the environment, batch-improvement gating) are truth-sensitive, and the batch-improvement gate operates at the run-to-run noise floor so its admissions flip under re-scoring.
Related Work: ReMe (arXiv:2512.10696) validates experiences with an LLM judge and prunes by utility; A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549) scores admission on future utility, factual confidence, novelty, recency and a content-type prior and reports store-level precision-recall on one conversational benchmark with no downstream task measurement; CraniMem (arXiv:2603.15642) uses goal-conditioned gating and utility tagging and reports robustness to injected distractors without analysing tagging errors; Compiled Memory / Atlas (arXiv:2603.15666) promotes verified sub-bullets through a three-step gate; batch-improvement gating admits mistake notes only when batch performance rises (arXiv:2512.11485); verifier-backed replay promotes skills into a graph (arXiv:2512.23760). On the threat side, MINJA (arXiv:2503.03704) and single-interaction steering (arXiv:2608.23471) inject records through queries; A-MemGuard (arXiv:2510.02373) defends with consensus validation and reports attack success rate only; FAMA (arXiv:2604.20006) shows agents reuse invalidated memories; the compliance-trap framework (arXiv:2607.10608) gives entry-propagation-recovery traces for harm attribution. The LLM-as-judge literature documents position, verbosity and style biases for answer grading (arXiv:2406.07791, arXiv:2506.13639, FairJudge arXiv:2602.06625) but never for memory admission, and RM benchmarks for memory management (arXiv:2601.11969) do not test truth sensitivity. None of these plants ground-truth-labelled wrong, stale and adversarial records into the write stream of an agent experience memory, crosses the truth label with a style manipulation, measures each gate's admission as a function of both, and connects admission to paired downstream success.
Abstract: Agent experience memories are increasingly protected by write-time admission gates, yet no gate has been audited for what it admits. We plant records of known truth value into the write stream of an ALFWorld experience memory and audit six gates: four that decide from the record's text (ReMe LLM-judge, A-MAC five-factor, CraniMem utility tagging, Atlas-style LLM verification) and two that reference execution (environment replay, batch-improvement gating). Because ALFWorld is deterministic, the correctness of a record's action recommendation is labelled exactly by replay. Planted classes cross truth with style: correct-styled, correct-plain, wrong, stale (true in the source scene, re-bound to a location from another scene) and adversarial (wrong records rewritten into the lexical style of the gate's own admitted set). We measure per-gate admission by class, fit admission on style features versus the truth label, build one store per gate from the same stream, and evaluate 400 held-out tasks in a paired design on the 27B dense and 120B MoE backbones, with entry-propagation-recovery traces attributing failures to admitted planted records and a matched-rate random-admission control separating gate selectivity from mere volume reduction. The central claim is that text-only gates are style classifiers whose store-level precision does not predict downstream success, that replay is the only truth-sensitive gate, and that the batch gate's decisions are dominated by evaluation noise. Costs per gated record are reported so that harm prevented can be priced against gate tokens.
Experiments: 1) Write stream: run the base agent (27B dense; audit replicated on the 120B MoE) on 700 ALFWorld training tasks and extract one candidate record per episode with a fixed ReMe-style extractor (condition, action plan, outcome, note). Ground truth per record by deterministic replay in the record's source scene: correct iff the recommended plan achieves the subgoal it claims. 2) Planted classes, each about 15 percent of the stream, restricted to replay-checkable content: (Cs) correct-styled; (Cp) correct-plain, the same records stripped of confidence phrasing and specificity markers; (W) wrong, records from failed trajectories with the outcome field flipped or with the object-receptacle binding swapped to a replay-verified false location; (S) stale, correct records re-bound to the receptacle from a different scene of the same room type; (A) adversarial, W records passed through a black-box style transfer into the style of the gate's top-admitted records, tuned on a disjoint calibration set. 3) Gates reimplemented locally: G1 ReMe LLM-judge; G2 A-MAC five-factor with cross-validated weights; G3 CraniMem utility tagging plus goal-conditioned gate; G4 Atlas-style three-step LLM verification without replay; G5 batch-improvement gate (admit iff a 32-task batch improves with the record present); G6 replay verification (execute the plan in the source scene). Bounds: G0 ungated, oracle (admit iff truth). 4) Admission analysis: admission rate by class with Wilson CIs; precision and recall against replay truth; logistic regression of admission on style features (length, specificity count, confidence lexicon, template match, embedding similarity to the admitted set) with and without the truth label, reporting AUC gain and a permutation test on the truth coefficient. 5) Downstream: for each gate build the store from admitted records only, retrieve top-3 by task-description embedding (k fixed at the pilot's safe dose), evaluate 400 held-out tasks (200 seen-scene, 200 unseen-scene) paired across all gates and G0, 3 seeds, both backbones; the downstream arm proceeds only if the 120B shows a store-versus-no-store delta above the pre-registered MDE. 6) Harm attribution: entry-propagation-recovery traces on every episode that retrieved a planted record; per-class harm as P(fail given planted retrieved and adopted) minus P(fail given a matched control retrieval). 7) Batch-gate noise: repeat G5's decision for 200 candidates with a second seed of the same batch and report the flip rate against G6's flip rate. 8) Cost: LLM tokens and environment steps per gated record and harm prevented per 1k gate tokens. Budget: about 12 stores x 400 tasks x 3 seeds per backbone, roughly 14k evaluation episodes per backbone plus gate calls.
Baselines and Ablations: G0 ungated store; oracle gate; random-admission gate matched to each gate's admission rate (isolates selectivity from volume); a style-only surrogate classifier trained on each gate's own decisions, tested for how well it reproduces them; G1 with a variant that re-reads the full source trajectory before judging; removing one planted class at a time from the admitted store to locate which class carries downstream harm; injection at k of 1 versus 3 to confirm harm depends on planted content rather than volume; the whole audit repeated with a second extractor (ExpeL-style insights) to show the finding is not extractor-specific; G5 at batch sizes 16, 32 and 64.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1: for G1 to G4, admission(A) is at least 0.8 times admission(Cs) and admission(Cp) is at most admission(A); style features alone reach AUC of at least 0.80 on admission and the truth label adds less than 0.05 AUC. Falsified if any text-only gate has a significant truth coefficient (permutation p below 0.01) with admission(A) below half of admission(Cs). P2: the ranking of G1 to G4 by store-level precision has Spearman rho at most 0.5 with their ranking by paired downstream success, and each is within MDE of its matched-rate random-admission control. Falsified if every text-only gate beats its random control by more than MDE. P3: G6 admits class A at 10 percent or less and is the only gate whose downstream delta over G0 exceeds MDE on the 120B; falsified if a text-only gate matches G6 downstream. P4: G5 decisions flip at 35 percent or more under seed re-scoring at batch 32; falsified if the flip rate is below 15 percent. P5 (secondary, may fail without threatening the main claim): downstream harm from admitted planted records concentrates in classes S and A rather than W, because W records mismatch retrieval conditions more often.
Measurement and Noise Control: Per-task paired outcomes across stores built from the same stream; McNemar exact test on discordant pairs; 3 seeds x 2 backbones; null replicates (G0 versus G0 under a different seed) calibrate the distribution of net flips; MDE pre-registered from pilot discordance (about 5 percentage points net at n=400 with 15 percent discordance), effects below MDE reported as null; task-level cluster bootstrap for the precision-versus-success rank correlation; at least 150 planted records per class with Wilson CIs on admission rates; all gate prompts, thresholds and the adversarial rewrite fixed before the confirmatory run, with the rewrite tuned on records disjoint from the audited stream; retrieval model and k identical across stores so only admitted content varies.

Name: dormant_is_not_dead
Title: Dormant Is Not Dead: Usage-Decay Forgetting in Agent Experience Memory Buys Stationary Savings with an Irreversible Loss at Task-Family Return
Short Hypothesis: Recency- and usage-decay pruning (FadeMem-style differential decay, ReMe utility pruning, CraniMem bounded buffers with scheduled consolidation) deletes exactly the records a task family needs when it returns after a dormant period: on a long ALFWorld stream with a return block, the success loss at return exceeds any stationary gain the pruning bought, is not closed by re-learning within the block, and is larger than the loss from random pruning to the same store size, whereas a redundancy-based (coverage-preserving, time-agnostic) prune at the same size keeps return-block success within noise of the unpruned store; the maintenance LLM calls of decay and consolidation policies cost more tokens than they save at read time.
Related Work: FadeMem (arXiv:2601.18642) applies adaptive decay across a dual-layer hierarchy and improves multi-hop QA while cutting storage, without testing recall failures on rarely accessed but later-critical items or any task-execution setting; ReMe (arXiv:2512.10696) prunes by utility; CraniMem (arXiv:2603.15642) keeps a bounded episodic buffer with scheduled consolidation and pruning; a retention schema with hybrid forgetting (arXiv:2512.12856) is evaluated in generative-agent simulation; MemCon (arXiv:2607.13591) learns when to consolidate or forget; Auto-Dreamer (arXiv:2605.20616) learns offline consolidation that abstracts recurring patterns and prunes redundant entries, the closest existing redundancy-based prune, but is not tested under a return to a dormant family; the stability-plasticity paper (arXiv:2604.27003) shows old and new experiences compete at retrieval; Capability-Preserving Evolution (arXiv:2605.09315) documents erosion under memory evolution and adds a constraint, without attributing erosion to a forgetting criterion; AgentCL (arXiv:2606.02461) proposes controlled task streams for continual-learning evaluation of language agents but compares no forgetting policies, has no return-block design and no reinsertion counterfactual; Evo-Memory (arXiv:2511.20857) and StreamMemBench (arXiv:2606.14571) are streaming benchmarks without forgetting-policy comparison; Memory Anchors (arXiv:2608.26545) prioritizes critical replay experiences in continual robot learning, an analogous concern in replay buffers rather than LLM experience stores; the write-manage-read survey (arXiv:2603.07670) warns that learned forgetting could delete safety-critical information; segment-level consolidation (arXiv:2608.12990) prices consolidation cost on QA. None measures the deletion of dormant-but-later-critical records on an agent task stream, compares recency-based against random and redundancy-based pruning at matched size, or accounts maintenance calls against read-time savings.
Abstract: Forgetting policies for agent memory are validated on short, stationary streams where deleting rarely used records is free. We test the case they never face: a task family that goes dormant and returns. On ALFWorld we run a 1,050-episode stream in seven blocks of 150, covering the six task families and then returning to the first, and grow one experience store per policy from the same fixed writer, capped at 30 percent of the unpruned size: recency decay (FadeMem-style), usage-utility pruning (ReMe-style), bounded FIFO with scheduled consolidation (CraniMem-style), a redundancy-based prune that keeps one representative per coverage cluster regardless of age, random pruning, the unpruned store, and a hindsight oracle. A fixed probe set stratified by family is evaluated before and after the return block, and the return block itself is scored in thirds to expose re-learning. Two diagnostics attribute any loss: reinserting the deleted family records at the start of the return block with the same seed, and counting deleted records that the unpruned run retrieved and adopted in successes where the pruned run failed. We predict that recency and usage pruning fall below the unpruned store at return by more than the minimum detectable effect, that random pruning loses less than they do, that reinsertion recovers most of the deficit, that redundancy pruning stays within noise of the unpruned store at the same size, and that decay and consolidation maintenance tokens exceed read-time savings. A no-return control stream and a return-distance sweep separate dormancy from generic drift. The result would replace time-since-use with redundancy as the deletion criterion for agent experience stores.
Experiments: 1) Stream: ALFWorld's six task families; 1,050 training episodes in blocks of 150 ordered A, B, C, D, E, F, A-prime, with A-prime returning to family A; the returning family is rotated across three rotations so the result is not family-specific; 415 held-out tasks form a fixed probe set stratified by family (about 69 per family). 2) Writer fixed across policies: after each episode one record is extracted with the same ReMe-style extractor; every policy is forced to the same cap, 30 percent of the unpruned store size at the end of block F. 3) Policies: F1 recency decay with access-based reinforcement (FadeMem-style); F2 usage-utility prune (retrieve count times success ratio, dormant records fall to zero); F3 bounded FIFO with scheduled consolidation (merge near-duplicates, drop oldest); F4 redundancy prune (embedding clusters, keep the medoid plus the best-outcome member, time-agnostic); F5 unpruned; F6 random prune to the cap; F7 hindsight oracle that keeps the records F5's run retrieved and adopted in successful A-prime episodes. 4) Measurement points: the probe is evaluated after block F and after A-prime for every policy; F1, F2 and F5 are also probed after every block to trace erosion; A-prime episodes are scored in thirds. 5) Reinsertion counterfactual: for F1 and F2, reinsert only the deleted family-A records at the start of A-prime and re-run A-prime with the same seed. 6) Dormant-critical rate: fraction of deleted records that F5's A-prime run retrieved and adopted in a success where the paired F1 or F2 episode failed. 7) Cost accounting: LLM tokens spent on decay updates, consolidation and utility maintenance per policy versus read-time tokens saved relative to F5, plus wall-clock. 8) Backbones: 120B MoE primary because the retrieval channel has measurable value there; 27B as a direction-only replication with one rotation. Secondary environment: WebShop with product-category blocks, same design, one seed. Budget: about 7 policies x 3 seeds x 1,050 stream episodes plus 7 policies x 2 checkpoints x 415 probes x 3 seeds for one rotation and F1, F4, F5 for the other two rotations, roughly 25k to 30k episodes on the 120B over a few days.
Baselines and Ablations: F5 unpruned, F6 random and F7 oracle as bounds; store cap swept at 15, 30 and 50 percent; return distance varied (A-prime after two blocks versus five) to trace the dependence on dormancy length; k of 1 versus 3 at read time; F4 with recency tie-breaking to test whether any temporal signal helps; extractor variant (raw trajectory records versus distilled records) to check that dormancy loss is not representation-specific; a no-return control stream (A through F then a fresh family G) where usage pruning should show no loss; a pre-gate that requires F5 minus no-memory on the probe to exceed MDE on the 120B before the confirmatory run.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1: on the post-return probe restricted to family A, F1 and F2 are below F5 by more than MDE (McNemar p below 0.05 in at least two of three rotations) and F4 is within MDE of F5. Falsified if F1 and F2 are within MDE of F5. P2: F6 (random, same size) loses less than F1 and F2 at return; falsified if random pruning is at least as bad. P3: reinsertion of the deleted family-A records recovers at least 70 percent of the F1 and F2 deficit; falsified if under 40 percent. P4: the last third of A-prime under F1 and F2 is still below F5 by more than MDE, so re-learning within 150 episodes does not close the gap. P5: over blocks B to F, F1 and F2 gain less over F5 than they lose at return, and for F1 and F3 maintenance tokens exceed read-time token savings; if F5 shows no distractor harm at this cap (plausible at k of 3), the only benefit of pruning is cost and it is negative for decay and consolidation policies. P6: on the no-return control stream, F1 and F2 are within MDE of F5, so the loss is specific to return rather than to pruning per se.

Name: abstraction_discards_bindings_and_repairs
Title: Abstraction Is Not the Variable, the Surviving Cues Are: Scene Bindings and Failure-to-Repair Pairs Explain When Distilled Experience Beats Raw Trajectories at Matched Tokens
Short Hypothesis: The published disagreement between SkillEvolBench (raw trajectory reuse beats distilled skills) and SEC (four-field records beat raw trajectories on ALFWorld) is not about abstraction level; it is about two cue classes that a representation either keeps or discards: scene bindings (which receptacle held the object), whose value exists only when evaluation scenes overlap training scenes and which reverse to harm on unseen scenes, and failure-to-repair pairs (what the successful trajectory did after a 'Nothing happens' or not-found), which transfer across scenes. At a matched injected-token budget, any representation that keeps both cues matches raw on seen scenes and beats raw on unseen scenes at a fraction of raw's tokens, and transplanting each cue into or out of a representation moves success by the predicted amount independent of the representation's nominal abstraction level.
Related Work: SkillEvolBench (arXiv:2605.24117) finds raw trajectory reuse often beats distilled skills 'due to discarded contextual cues' but names no cue, matches no budget and reports no split by scene overlap; SEC (Experience Retrieval Compression, AIEA 2026) distills each trajectory into task type, key decisions, failure reason and repair action and reports about +7.7 over raw on ALFWorld, notably retaining the failure-to-repair cue; ExpeL insights (the +9 joint cell in the brief); Demystifying Agent Skills (arXiv:2608.14036) argues skills help by procedural anchoring rather than by injecting missing knowledge, a mechanism that predicts no seen-versus-unseen asymmetry for raw's advantage and therefore contrasts with this proposal; Trace2Skill (arXiv:2603.25158) consolidates trajectory-local lessons into declarative skills; HORM (arXiv:2606.11680) links summaries to raw trajectories; AdaMEM (arXiv:2606.05684) hybridizes raw long-term and strategy short-term memory; the memory-structure study (arXiv:2412.15266) shows structure matters and mixed memory is most resilient, on external text with QA metrics; substrate routing (arXiv:2608.15008); hierarchical skill bases from stronger agents (arXiv:2604.04804, arXiv:2608.07169); the storage-reflection-experience taxonomy (arXiv:2605.06716) asks exactly when abstraction beats raw without measuring it; SIT-Graph (arXiv:2512.07287) stores episodic summaries on tool-graph edges; contextual drag (arXiv:2602.04288) shows failed attempts in context bias later generations, which bears on whether failure-to-repair pairs help or hurt. None names the cue classes inside items, transplants them across representations at matched tokens, or splits results by scene overlap.
Abstract: Studies of experience-memory representation disagree: SkillEvolBench reports that raw trajectories beat distilled skills, SEC reports that compact four-field records beat raw trajectories, and taxonomies ask when abstraction wins without measuring it. We propose that the abstraction level is not the operative variable. From one pool of successful ALFWorld trajectories we materialize six representations (raw, indexed summary, insight, skill, SEC-style record, state graph) and annotate each item, exactly from the logs, for two cue classes: scene bindings (object-to-receptacle facts from the source scene) and failure-to-repair pairs (the corrective action after a failed step). We inject each representation at matched token budgets on seen-scene and unseen-scene evaluation tasks in a paired design on the 27B dense and 120B MoE backbones, and we transplant each cue into and out of raw, insight and SEC-style records. The predictions are sharp: raw beats insight on seen scenes and not on unseen scenes; masking bindings removes most of raw's seen-scene advantage and appending a 60-token binding table to insights restores it; foreign bindings on unseen scenes are actively harmful, mediated by first-move adoption of the wrong receptacle; stripping repair pairs from SEC-style records removes most of SEC's gain on both splits while adding them to insights gains on both; and after conditioning on the two cue indicators the residual effect of representation is within noise. A budget crossover below one raw trajectory and a relevance-matched decoy control separate content from load. The outcome would turn 'which abstraction level' into 'which cues survive, and does the deployment scene overlap the training scene'.
Experiments: 1) Pool: successful trajectories from 1,000 training tasks produced by the 120B agent, with ALFWorld expert demonstrations as a second pool; the same pool feeds every representation. 2) Representations built by fixed local prompts on the 27B with the writer held constant: R1 raw trajectory; R2 indexed summary (60-token summary plus step index with on-demand dereference within budget, HORM-like); R3 insight (ExpeL-style cross-trajectory rules); R4 skill (parameterized procedure, Trace2Skill-like); R5 SEC-style four-field record; R6 serialized state/tool graph (SIT-Graph-like). 3) Cue annotation from the logs: an item contains a scene binding if it states an object-receptacle pair matching the source scene's ground truth; it contains a failure-to-repair pair if it states an action that returned 'Nothing happens' or not-found followed by the corrective action; both checks are deterministic on ALFWorld. 4) Transplants on R1, R3 and R5: plus-B (append a binding table from the source scene, at most 60 tokens), minus-B (replace receptacle identities with placeholders), plus-R (append mined failure-to-repair pairs), minus-R (strip them); raw minus-B minus-R is the load-matched content-stripped control. 5) Budget: injected tokens matched at 400, 1,200 and 3,000 by top-k retrieval on task-description embeddings with truncation, k adapting to budget per representation; the main factorial runs at 1,200, the crossover sweep runs base representations only. 6) Evaluation: 200 seen-scene tasks (rooms present in the pool, different task instances) and 200 unseen-scene tasks (rooms absent from the pool), paired across every cell, 3 seeds, 120B primary and 27B replication. 7) Analysis: conditional logistic model with task fixed effects and terms for representation, split, cue indicators, budget and the cue-by-split interactions; the residual representation main effect after conditioning on cues is the 'abstraction per se' estimate. 8) Trace mediation: on unseen scenes, count episodes whose first navigation targets the binding location named in a retrieved item and fails, versus matched control episodes. 9) Secondary: WebShop with bindings defined as attribute-to-option mappings within a product category (seen) versus across categories (unseen), one seed. Budget: about 21 cells at 1,200 tokens (6 base, 12 transplant, 3 controls) x 400 tasks x 3 seeds, about 25k episodes on the 120B, plus a smaller crossover sweep and the 27B replication with 2 seeds.
Baselines and Ablations: No-memory agent; ExpeL joint (insights plus retrieved raw) as the published mixed baseline; SEC as published and SEC minus-R; raw at k of 1 versus truncated raw; a relevance-matched decoy (raw trajectory from a different task family in the same scene) to separate binding content from token load; the binding table appended to a hand-written instruction rather than to a memory item, testing whether the cue helps in the instruction slot; a third candidate cue (action ordering constraints) annotated and tested only if residual representation effects survive; the second pool (expert demos) to check that the cue effects are not specific to the 120B's own trajectories.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1: at 1,200 tokens or more, raw beats insight on seen scenes by more than MDE while insight is at least as good as raw on unseen scenes; the split-by-representation interaction is significant (p below 0.01). Falsified if there is no interaction. P2: raw minus-B loses at least 70 percent of raw's seen-scene advantage and insight plus-B recovers at least 70 percent of it at 25 percent or less of raw's tokens. Falsified if masking bindings leaves raw's seen advantage intact, in which case the repair-pair arm remains as the second candidate and the binding claim is dropped. P3: on unseen scenes, raw plus-B with foreign bindings is below raw minus-B by more than MDE, and first-move adoption of the named receptacle mediates at least half of the added failures. P4: SEC minus-R loses more than half of SEC's gain over raw on both splits and insight plus-R gains on both splits, with the plus-R effect split-invariant; falsified if stripping repair pairs leaves SEC's gain intact. P5: after conditioning on the two cue indicators, residual representation main effects are within MDE of zero; falsified if a residual effect above MDE survives for skill or graph. P6: at 400 tokens, raw is below every distilled form on both splits, because truncated raw loses the repair pair that sits late in the trajectory.
Measurement and Noise Control: Paired per-task outcomes with McNemar exact tests for pairwise cells and a conditional logistic model with task fixed effects for the factorial; 3 seeds; null replicates (same cell, different seed) calibrate the net-flip distribution; MDE pre-registered from pilot discordance (about 5 percentage points net at n of 400); cue annotation is deterministic from logs; retriever, query and embedding model are identical across cells so only item content varies; transplants are applied before retrieval and items are re-trimmed to the same token band so budgets stay matched; the decoy control isolates load; the cue-transplant order and thresholds are fixed before the confirmatory run.

Name: stale_true_state_facts_redaction
Title: Stale-True, Not Wrong: Episode-Specific State Facts Carry the Natural Harm of Agent Experience Memory, and Fact-Level Redaction Beats Abstention
Short Hypothesis: In an organically accumulated ALFWorld experience bank, the items that hurt are not procedurally wrong items but procedurally right items carrying state facts (object-receptacle placements, open/closed states) that were true in the source episode and are false in the target task. Per-task harm scales with the number of stale-true facts injected, not with injected tokens; the compliance-trap entry point is the first navigation action, which targets a receptacle named in a stale fact; and a read-time redaction that replaces state facts with typed placeholders at matched token length removes the harm at zero clean-task cost, whereas abstention, utility filtering and provenance gating buy safety with clean-task loss.
Related Work: arXiv:2607.10608 (Compliance Trap, E-P-R) diagnoses entry-point adoption of task-wrong memory, but only for deliberately injected conflicts and with no control policy. arXiv:2602.04288 (contextual drag) and arXiv:2605.10828 (nonlinear hard-distractor effect) show harm from in-task failures and from retrieved documents, not from an agent's own cross-episode experience. arXiv:2604.27003 reports that raw trajectories hinder adaptation while abstract insights are safer and that negative transfer concentrates on hard cases, but gives no fact-level mechanism and tests no read-time control. AdaMEM (arXiv:2606.05684) observes that start-of-episode guidance can point to the wrong receptacle and refreshes the strategy mid-episode, without labeling which injected facts were stale against ground truth. The Trap of Trajectory (arXiv:2605.09330, verified) is the closest neighbour: it frames agentic-memory failures as reliance on spurious patterns of three types and proposes CAMEL, a write- and retrieval-time calibration that reduces that reliance while preserving clean performance; it does not label organically retrieved facts against environment ground truth, does not separate stale-true facts from wrong procedures, and does not compare a fact-level redaction against abstention and filtering at matched tokens with clean-task cost accounting. Belief Memory (arXiv:2605.05583, verified) keeps multiple candidate conclusions with probabilities to avoid self-reinforcing errors, a different mechanism. ExpeL reports retrieve-only 55 / insights-only 50 / both 59 on ALFWorld without a harm analysis; SkillEvolBench and SEC compare raw versus distilled items without explaining why distillation sometimes wins. MemRL utility filtering (arXiv:2601.03192), provenance control (arXiv:2608.10509) and steerable reliance (arXiv:2601.05107) are candidate controls never compared on task execution. The program's pilot found that a 7-item injection fixed zero and broke six to seven items and that k=3 removed the harm.
Abstract: Negative transfer from agent experience memory has been diagnosed with deliberately injected conflicts, in-task failed attempts, or misleading external documents; how much harm an organically accumulated bank causes, and through which items, is unmeasured. We build an experience bank over an ALFWorld task stream with a standard success-gated write path, retrieve it for a disjoint evaluation set, and label every injected item post hoc against the target task's ground-truth initial state, which is available from the game file. This yields a deterministic, LLM-judge-free label for each stored fact (true-in-target or stale) and for each item (right, stale-true, wrong, conflicting). We claim that the harm is carried by stale-true facts inside procedurally correct items: per-task net failure flips are explained by the count of stale facts and not by injected tokens, and the first divergent action in harmed episodes targets a receptacle named in a stale fact at well above the rate of a permuted-fact control. We then compare read-time controls head to head at matched k and matched tokens: typed-placeholder redaction of state facts, permuted facts, oracle facts, abstention, utility filtering, provenance gating and reliance steering, each on clean and on stale tasks separately. The prediction is that redaction alone removes the harm at the same k that produced it without paying on clean tasks. The design directly tests the program's earlier conclusion that volume rather than content was the lever.
Experiments: 1) Bank construction: 800 ALFWorld training tasks (scenes disjoint from a 600-task evaluation set), 27B dense open-weight ReAct agent; bank stores successful raw trajectories and ExpeL-style insights; admission on environment success; retrieval by task-description embedding, k in {3, 7}. 2) Fact extraction and ground-truth labeling: regex over ALFWorld observation templates extracts (object, receptacle) and (receptacle, open/closed) facts from each stored trajectory; each fact is compared with the evaluation task's ground-truth initial state; items are labeled right, stale-true, wrong (task-family mismatch) or conflicting (contradicts another injected item). 3) Harm census: paired no-memory versus memory runs (k=7) on 600 tasks x 3 seeds; per-task net flip regressed on stale-fact count, token count and item-type counts; leave-one-item-out on a 150-task probe for per-item harm. 4) E-P-R traces: with fixed seeds and prefix-matched decoding, locate the first action divergence between memory and no-memory runs and classify whether it targets a stale-fact receptacle; compare against the permuted-fact control. 5) Read-time controls at matched k=7 and matched tokens: (a) redaction, receptacle identifiers in state facts replaced by typed placeholders and padded to equal length; (b) permuted facts, random receptacle names of the same type; (c) oracle facts, the true target placements; (d) abstention with a swept similarity threshold; (e) MemRL-style per-item utility filtering estimated on the stream; (f) provenance gating to same scene family or same task family; (g) reliance-steering instruction; (h) a CAMEL-style calibration reimplemented from arXiv:2605.09330 if its three pattern types are reproducible locally. Each control is scored separately on clean tasks (zero stale facts retrieved) and stale tasks. 6) Controlled dose: injections constructed with 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 stale facts at fixed tokens. 7) Backbones: 8B and 120B MoE replications for the stronger-agents-lose-more claim.

Name: utility_pruning_is_frequency_pruning
Title: Utility Pruning Is Frequency Pruning: Outcome-Based Refinement of Agent Experience Deletes Rare-Task Coverage, and the Bill Arrives Only After Distribution Shift
Short Hypothesis: The per-item utility estimates used to prune experience banks (success/failure counters in ReMe-style refinement, runtime RL utilities in MemRL, utility tags, recency decay) are confounded with how often an item's task family appears in the stream, so pruning under a store cap preferentially deletes items covering rare families. On a stationary evaluation this is invisible or slightly positive; after a shift toward the rare families the pruned bank loses a share of memory's value that exceeds run-to-run noise, and a frequency-normalized or redundancy-based pruning rule at the same cap removes most of the loss without giving up the stationary gain.
Related Work: ReMe (arXiv:2512.10696) prunes low-utility entries and reports a smaller model with memory beating a larger memoryless model, with no shift test and no per-family survival analysis. MemRL (arXiv:2601.03192) learns runtime utilities and itself notes drift toward reflection-like behavior at low task similarity. CraniMem (arXiv:2603.15642) uses utility tagging with scheduled pruning; active forgetting (arXiv:2601.18642) uses differential decay; neither measures what is deleted that is later needed. Capability-Preserving Evolution (arXiv:2605.09315) documents non-monotonic erosion under adaptation and fixes it with a retained-capability constraint, without effect sizes against noise and without isolating pruning as the cause. arXiv:2604.27003 frames old-versus-new experience competition as stability-plasticity at retrieval but compares no pruning policies. The experience-following study (arXiv:2505.16067, ACL 2025, verified) studies addition and deletion operations and error propagation through misaligned replay but does not measure collateral loss under a later shift. RoMeRL (arXiv:2608.02508, verified) compresses trajectory-indexed utilities into reduced-order per-task states to limit persistent reward contamination, a memory-reward trap, not a frequency confound. Mistake Notebook Learning (arXiv:2512.11485) admits notes only when batch performance improves, which carries the same frequency confound at admission. MemCon (arXiv:2607.13591) learns when to consolidate or forget without a swept static control. Archived program ideas memory_item_value_reliability, coverage_currency_coupling and breadth_routed_memory are adjacent and addressed below.
Abstract: Utility-based pruning, decay and consolidation are the standard answers to memory growth in self-improving agents, and every recent system reports that pruning keeps the pool compact without hurting accuracy. We argue that this conclusion is an artifact of stationary evaluation. Per-item utility is estimated from outcomes accumulated over retrievals, and retrieval frequency is dominated by how often the item's task family appears in the stream, so utility pruning is frequency pruning in disguise: it deletes items that cover rare families regardless of their per-use value. On ALFWorld we build banks over skewed task streams (four common families, two rare, rotated across designs), enforce a fixed store cap with seven pruning policies including ReMe-style counters, MemRL-style credited utilities, recency decay, random pruning, a frequency-normalized utility and a redundancy rule, and evaluate per-family success on fixed held-out sets before and after a designed shift toward the rare families. We measure the confound directly (utility versus family frequency, controlling for a leave-one-out estimate of per-use value) and the collateral cost as the post-shift rare-family loss relative to an unpruned bank and to a null replicate. The claim is falsified if rare-family items survive pruning at the same rate as common ones, or if the post-shift loss sits inside the noise band. A positive result qualifies the ReMe and MemRL pruning claims and gives a same-cap fix.
Experiments: 1) Stream design: six ALFWorld task families; phase A is 900 tasks drawn with family weights 0.22, 0.22, 0.22, 0.22, 0.06, 0.06 (the rare pair rotated across three designs so every family is rare in one); phase B is 300 tasks with the rare pair at weight 0.5; a control continuation keeps the phase-A mixture (no shift). 2) Bank: raw trajectories plus distilled insights, admission on success; store cap C=100 (also 50 and 200) enforced by the policy every 50 tasks. 3) Pruning policies at equal cap: (a) none, unbounded; (b) ReMe-style success-minus-failure counter over uses; (c) MemRL-style outcome-credited EMA with credit split across co-retrieved items; (d) recency decay; (e) frequency-normalized utility (utility divided by family exposure, pruning the bottom rank within each family); (f) redundancy pruning (drop the item with the highest nearest-neighbor similarity); (g) random pruning. 4) Evaluation: fixed held-out set of 100 tasks per family, scored after phase A and after phase B, paired across policies, plus a no-memory baseline. 5) Confound measurement: Spearman correlation between per-item utility and family frequency, controlling for a leave-one-out per-use utility estimated on a 150-task probe; per-family survival curves under each policy. 6) Retrieval ablation: family-aware retrieval to test whether the loss is store coverage or retrieval competition. 7) Backbones: 27B dense as main; 8B replication; 3 stream orders x 3 seeds.
Baselines and Ablations: No memory; unbounded bank; random pruning at the same cap (separates any pruning from utility pruning); cap sweep 50/100/200; k sweep 3/7; distilled-only versus raw-plus-distilled banks; family-blind versus family-aware retrieval; frequency-normalized utility versus redundancy pruning as the two candidate fixes; no-shift continuation as the temporal control.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1: Spearman correlation between per-item utility and family frequency is at least 0.4 after controlling for probe-estimated per-use utility, and rare-family item survival under policies (b), (c) and (d) is at most half of common-family survival at equal cap; falsified if survival is family-independent. P2: After phase A, (b) and (c) are inside the null band of (a) or better on the held-out set. P3: After phase B, rare-family success under (b), (c) and (d) is below (a) by at least 3 null-replicate standard deviations of the per-family metric, and (e) and (f) recover at least half of that gap at the same cap; falsified if (b) matches (a) on rare families post-shift or if (e) and (f) do not beat (b). P4: Random pruning (g) loses on common and rare families alike, whereas utility pruning loses only on rare families, the signature of frequency bias rather than capacity. P5: The loss is store coverage, not retrieval competition: family-aware retrieval does not shrink the gap between (b) and (a).
Measurement and Noise Control: Per-family success on fixed held-out sets, paired across policies at identical stream order and seed; a null replicate (policy (a) run twice with different seeds on the same stream) sets the per-family standard deviation and the minimum detectable effect before confirmatory runs; 3 stream orders x 3 seeds; the reported quantity is the mean and spread of the rare-family delta, never a single best run; k and item length caps are fixed so per-task token cost is equal across policies; admission and retrieval code are shared; the no-shift continuation separates shift-induced loss from time-on-stream drift; thresholds pre-registered.

Risk Factors and Limitations: Six ALFWorld families are a coarse notion of a rare task, and the shift is designed rather than organic. Some utility implementations already normalize by exposure, in which case the confound is smaller than claimed and P1 fails informatively. Name: failure_memory_framing_drag
Title: The Note Is the Dose: Cross-Episode Failure Memory Induces Contextual Drag in Agent Execution, and Positive Rewriting, Not Failure Labeling, Removes It
Short Hypothesis: When failure-derived memory (failed trajectories, mistake notes, avoid-style insights) is retrieved from other episodes, the agent reproduces the flagged error class at a rate that rises with the amount of verbatim erroneous action content in the item, regardless of the explicit failure label. A positive rewrite that states the corrected procedure without reproducing the erroneous actions keeps the corrective value and removes the drag. The benefit reported for failure memory therefore depends on framing rather than on the presence of failure information, and the common negation framing sits in the harmful region.
Related Work: Contextual drag (arXiv:2602.04288) shows in-task failed attempts bias later generations toward structurally similar errors on reasoning tasks, with 10-20 percent drops across 11 models, and that neither feedback nor self-verification removes it; cross-episode retrieved memory is untested. Why Retrying Fails (arXiv:2605.08563) documents context contamination on retry within an agent pipeline. Mistake Notebook Learning (arXiv:2512.11485) distills batch-clustered failures into notes admitted when batch performance improves, without varying the note's framing. Learning from Failure for computer-use agents (arXiv:2606.31270) turns failed trajectories into LLM diagnoses and code patches, again without a framing variable. ExpeL derives insights from success/failure comparisons, many phrased as avoid rules; Reflexion stores verbal reflections on the agent's own failures. arXiv:2607.13884 produces correction insights by graph matching failed and expert trajectories, a positive-corrective form never compared against negation framing. ReMe includes failure-trigger analysis as one distillation facet. arXiv:2509.25370 offers an agent error taxonomy. Memory-Induced Tool-Drift (arXiv:2605.24941, verified) concerns personality biases in long-term memory leaking into tool calls, a different phenomenon. The failure-attribution line (AgentRx arXiv:2602.02475, FALAT arXiv:2606.00765, OAT arXiv:2607.12747) localizes failure steps but does not study their reuse as memory. Archived program ideas memory_induced_shortcutting, action_prior_imprinting and memory_vetoes_instruction_slot concern different mechanisms.
Abstract: Failure-derived memory is a standard component of self-improving agents: failed trajectories, mistake notes and avoid rules are stored and retrieved on the premise that showing the agent what went wrong prevents repetition. Contextual drag shows the opposite for in-task failures on reasoning problems: errors in context are inherited. We test whether the drag transfers to cross-episode retrieved failure memory during task execution and whether it is governed by how the failure is written. On ALFWorld we define five error classes with deterministic trace detectors (loops, precondition violations, missing required sub-steps, wrong goal receptacle, invalid actions), collect organic failures from a training stream, and derive from each failure four content-matched items: a verbatim labeled failure excerpt, a negation note, a positive rewrite of the corrected procedure, and a contrastive pair. Holding retrieval, k and tokens fixed, we measure the rate at which the retrieved item's error class recurs in the agent's own trace, its structural similarity to the injected erroneous steps, and task success, with a matched success trajectory and a no-memory baseline. The central prediction is a monotone ordering, verbatim failure worst, negation intermediate, positive rewrite best, and a within-item dose effect of verbatim erroneous steps at fixed tokens. If negation notes match positive rewrites, or failures never raise reproduction, the claim fails. The result would locate the value of failure memory in its framing and give a write-time rule that costs nothing at read time.
Experiments: 1) Error classes with deterministic detectors on ALFWorld traces: E1 loop (re-opening or re-examining the same receptacle at least twice without new information), E2 precondition violation (put before take; acting on a closed receptacle), E3 missing required sub-step (placing without clean, heat or cool; examining without turning on the lamp), E4 goal-receptacle error, E5 invalid action string. 2) Failure bank: 27B dense agent on 800 training tasks without memory; failed trajectories collected and auto-labeled by error class; the local model derives from each failure four framings with content held constant: F1 verbatim failure excerpt with a FAILED label, F2 negation note (do not X before Y), F3 positive rewrite (corrected procedure only), F4 contrastive (F1 plus F3); F2 and F3 length-matched within 10 percent, F1 and F4 comparisons padded with neutral filler; S is a matched successful trajectory of the same family. 3) Retrieval: for each of 500 held-out tasks, top-3 items of the assigned framing by task-description similarity; conditions none, S, F1, F2, F3, F4 at equal k and token budget. 4) Metrics: reproduction rate of the retrieved item's error class in the agent's trace (primary), normalized edit distance between the injected erroneous subsequence and the agent's trace (structural imitation), task success (secondary). 5) Dose sweep within F1: 1, 3 or 5 erroneous steps at fixed total tokens. 6) In-task versus cross-task: append the agent's own failed attempt (in-task, replicating arXiv:2602.04288 in execution) and compare drag magnitude with a stranger's retrieved failure of the same class. 7) Backbones: 8B, 27B dense, 120B MoE.
Baselines and Ablations: No memory; matched success trajectory S; F1 through F4; F1 with the FAILED label removed (does the label matter); F2 with erroneous actions paraphrased at the action-type level without verbatim command strings; relevance control with items from an unrelated family (does drag require relevance); token-matched filler; an instruction-only baseline containing a generic verify-preconditions rule (checks that F3's benefit is not a generic reminder); dose sweep within F1.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1: Reproduction rate under F1 is at least 1.5 times the rate under no memory and above the rate under S on tasks where the error class is applicable; falsified if F1 is at or below no memory. P2: Ordering F1 > F2 > none >= F3, with F3 significantly below none; falsified if F2 is indistinguishable from F3. P3: Within F1, reproduction rate rises monotonically with the number of verbatim erroneous steps at fixed tokens; falsified if flat. P4: Success ordering F3 >= F4 > none >= F2 > F1 on applicable tasks, and all conditions inside the null band on non-applicable tasks (no generic load effect at matched tokens). P5: Cross-episode drag is at least half the magnitude of in-task drag for the same error class; falsified if cross-episode reproduction equals no memory. P6: Removing the FAILED label from F1 changes reproduction by no more than the null band (the label is not protective).
Measurement and Noise Control: Paired per-task comparisons across framings on the same 500 tasks; McNemar tests on reproduction and on success; per-error-class stratification with pre-registered minimum stratum counts; 3 seeds per condition; a null replicate (no memory versus no memory across seeds) fixes the reproduction-rate floor and the minimum detectable effect before confirmatory runs; detectors are deterministic and need no LLM judge; framings are generated once and audited by a second local model for content equivalence (same error class, same correction), with disagreements dropped rather than adjudicated; retrieval, k, tokens, template and temperature are shared across conditions; roughly 6 conditions x 500 tasks x 3 seeds plus the dose sweep, about 12k episodes, fits the single-node budget.

Name: harm_does_not_distill
Title: Gain Distills, Harm Does Not: Context Distillation Is an Asymmetric Filter on Agent Experience, and What That Says About Where Memory Harm Lives
Short Hypothesis: For one fixed experience pool, moving it from the context window into LoRA weights by context distillation preserves the pool's in-context gain but not its high-dose harm: a student distilled from a teacher that consumes the harmful k=7 bank ends up statistically indistinguishable (paired, item-level) from a student distilled from the benign k=3 teacher and shows no one-sided break signature, because the harm is a read-time interference between the specific retrieved items and the current query rather than a behavioral disposition carried by the teacher's outputs. If instead the harm is dispositional (shortcutting, majority-action prior), the k=7 student must inherit it.
Related Work: Experience Distillation (arXiv:2607.21051, 2026-07) is the closest: context distillation of an agent's own interaction histories retains at least 64.8% of in-context gains on 749 SWE tasks and six text games while direct SFT on the same experience recovers only 3.8%; it fixes one dose, reports means only, and never asks whether in-context harm is retained. PMD (arXiv:2607.01480) distills a three-level procedural memory into policy weights via a memory-conditioned self-teacher but never compares against keeping the same memory in context; SIRI (arXiv:2606.02355) and PEAM (arXiv:2605.27762) internalize skills and report gains over retrieval baselines without a matched-pool, matched-cost control; arXiv:2606.04703 finds off-policy context distillation on high-quality teacher trajectories is the stable internalization regime and that instance-level experience collapses under iteration, again without a harm measurement; CardDistill in SkillLens (arXiv:2608.10775) and DuoMem (arXiv:2606.29961) use privileged teacher context to train retrieval-free students in GUI and on-device settings. MemRL (arXiv:2601.03192), RLEM (arXiv:2306.07929) and hierarchical teacher-memory injection (arXiv:2608.07169) are the in-context side and each lacks the fine-tune-on-the-same-pool comparison named by G26. The Compliance Trap (arXiv:2607.10608) and the pilot's own k=7 result establish that in-context harm exists; neither asks whether it survives a change of substrate.
Abstract: Experience memories and weight-space distillation are treated as interchangeable routes to the same knowledge, but the program's pilot showed the in-context route has a dose-dependent harm channel: seven retrieved items broke six to seven held-out tasks and fixed none, three items did not. We use that harm as a probe of the substrate. From one pool of trajectories collected by the base model on the training split of ALFWorld, we materialize experience four ways at matched training compute and report inference cost: in context at k in {1,3,7}; direct SFT on pool successes; context distillation from a teacher consuming k=3; and context distillation from a teacher consuming the harmful k=7, trained on all teacher outputs (not success-filtered) so that any dispositional harm has a path into the weights. Paired item-level evaluation on held-out tasks tests two pre-registered claims: (1) the k=3 student retains at least half of the in-context gain at zero injected tokens, replicating and cost-normalizing Experience Distillation; (2) the k=7 student is within an equivalence margin of the k=3 student and shows no one-sided break signature, whereas in-context k=7 does. Outcome (2) would locate memory harm on the read path (query-item interference under load) and imply that distillation is an asymmetric filter that keeps content and discards interference; its rejection would show the harm is a learned disposition, which is what the shortcutting and action-prior accounts predict. Either result is a substrate-level fact that no current parametric-memory paper measures, and it is obtained on 7B and 27B open models on one node.
Experiments: Backbone: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as primary (used by SIRI and 2603.18272), Gemma-3-27B (27B dense class already run in this program) as replicate. Pool: task-type-stratified split of the 1,465 local ALFWorld tasks into ~1,000 train / ~465 held-out plus the 134 unseen-scene eval tasks; the base ReAct agent runs each train task up to three attempts with a brief reflection, yielding a pool of successful and failed raw trajectories; the same pool is frozen for all arms. Gate 0 (pre-registered): reproduce the dose effect on this backbone by sweeping k in {0,1,3,7,11} raw trajectories retrieved by task-description embedding; the harmful dose k_h is the smallest k whose paired broken-minus-fixed count is positive with McNemar p<0.05; if none exists up to k=11 the asymmetry claim is declared untestable on this backbone and the study reports retained value and cost only. Parametric arms, all LoRA (rank 32, same optimizer, same number of target tokens, wall-clock GPU-hours logged): P-SFT, direct SFT on pool successes; P-CD3, off-policy context distillation, teacher = base + k=3 retrieval generating on train tasks, student trained on the teacher outputs with the retrieved block removed from the prompt (cross-entropy on teacher tokens plus optional KL to teacher logits); P-CDh, same with the teacher at k_h; P-CD3-succ and P-CDh-succ, success-filtered variants (ablation that closes the harm path by construction). Evaluation: each arm on the 465 held-out tasks x 5 seeds and the 134 unseen-scene tasks x 5 seeds, paired by task and seed across arms; optional two-fold cross-fitting (swap train and held-out halves) to double the paired sample. Measures: success rate; per-task fixed/broken counts versus the k=0 base (McNemar and bootstrap CIs); the harm signature = broken minus fixed; episode length, number of exploration actions before the first task-relevant commit, and action n-gram overlap with the retrieved items (the shortcutting and imitation probes); prompt and generated tokens per episode; GPU-hours of training. Stacking cell: P-CD3 evaluated with k=3 at inference, to test whether in-context and parametric value add or substitute. Mechanism cell: in-context k_h with relevance-matched decoy trajectories from other task types (length-matched load without content) to confirm that the harm reproduced under Gate 0 is load-driven as in the pilot.
Baselines and Ablations: Baselines: k=0 base; in-context k=1,3,k_h; P-SFT (the 3.8%-recovery reference from 2607.21051); ExpeL-style insight injection at matched tokens as a distilled-in-context reference. Ablations: success-filtered versus all-output distillation (closes the harm path); LoRA rank 16/32/64 and half training steps (does retained value scale with capacity); KL-to-teacher versus token cross-entropy; teacher outputs sampled at temperature 0 versus 0.7; second backbone (27B); length-matched decoy in-context arm; stacking cell P-CD3 + k=3; a P-CDh student additionally evaluated with the k_h bank in context (does a distilled student become more or less vulnerable to the same bank).
Falsifiable Predictions: P1 (retained value): P-CD3 recovers at least 50% of the in-context k=3 gain over base on the paired held-out set with zero injected memory tokens, and P-SFT recovers less than 25%; rejected if P-CD3's retained fraction has an upper 95% CI below 50%. P2 (asymmetry, the central claim): the paired difference P-CDh minus P-CD3 lies inside a pre-registered equivalence margin of +/-3 points (TOST at alpha 0.05), and P-CDh's broken-minus-fixed count versus base is not significantly positive, while in-context k_h reproduces the one-sided signature under Gate 0; rejected if P-CDh is below P-CD3 by more than 3 points with a one-sided break pattern, which would mean the harm is dispositional and distills. P3 (mechanism consistency): if P2 holds, P-CDh's episode length and pre-commit exploration count are within noise of P-CD3's, and the decoy in-context arm reproduces at least half of the k_h harm; if P2 fails, P-CDh shows the shortened episodes of the k_h teacher. P4 (cost): at equal or better success, P-CD3 uses at least 40% fewer prompt tokens per episode than in-context k=3, and the break-even number of evaluation episodes after which distillation training cost is amortized is under 2,000. P5 (exploratory, not confirmatory): stacking P-CD3 with k=3 in context yields less than 30% of the original k=3 gain on top, i.e. the two substrates substitute rather than add.
Measurement and Noise Control: All contrasts are paired by task and seed; 465 held-out tasks x 5 seeds gives an expected minimum detectable paired difference of roughly 3-4 points at 80% power (computed at pre-registration from the base run's per-task variance), so every confirmatory threshold is set at or above it and every predicted null is tested as equivalence with a stated margin, never as a failure to reject. Noise floor: two independently seeded training runs of P-CD3 and two of P-SFT are compared against each other as null replicates, giving the arm-level run-to-run band that any parametric contrast must exceed; the in-context arms get the same treatment by re-scoring one candidate twice (the program's 0.05-0.14 band). One-sidedness is tested with McNemar on discordant pairs and reported with the raw fixed/broken counts. Gate 0 fixes k_h before any parametric run and is filed with the thresholds; amendments after the first confirmatory run are logged. Cost is reported as tokens per episode and GPU-hours per arm, not as a ratio.

Name: memory_in_the_loop_training_decomposition
Title: Crutch, Content, or Read Skill? A Train-by-Infer 2x2 with Bank Swap Decomposes What Memory-in-the-Loop Training Actually Teaches an Agent
Short Hypothesis: When an agent is fine-tuned with retrieved experience in its context (retrieval-aware SFT, memory-tool RL), the reported gain over an untrained memoryless base decomposes into content absorbed from the training trajectories (available with memory removed), the untrained read benefit an unmodified backbone gets from the same bank, and a learned read skill equal to the interaction term. We claim the interaction term is within an equivalence margin of zero, that the trained model is bank-co-adapted (it loses more than the untrained model when its bank is swapped for an equally good disjoint bank), and that stripped of memory it underperforms a model trained on identical trajectories with the memory removed from the training context: memory in the training loop is a crutch that displaces internalization, not a skill.
Related Work: Retrieval-Augmented LLM Agents: Learning to Learn from Experience (arXiv:2603.18272) establishes a LoRA SFT recipe, analyses retrieval design and integrates experience retrieval into fine-tuning, reporting better unseen-task generalization; it reports the SFT-only and retrieval-in-training cells but not the retrieval-trained model evaluated without retrieval or with a swapped bank. MemHarness (arXiv:2607.28272) trains a GRPO policy to reconstruct retrieved experience and claims the objective improves intrinsic (memory-free) reasoning, without a control trained on the same rollouts with memory stripped. AgeMem (arXiv:2601.01885) folds memory operations into the policy and beats heuristic-controller baselines whose training differs; skill-integrated RL (arXiv:2512.17102) and UCOB (arXiv:2606.29502, +23.5 on ALFWorld over skill-free RL) compare against RL that saw different data; SLEA-RL (arXiv:2603.18079) retrieves step-level experience during RL. All of these are exactly the confound G27 names. RAFT-style mixed training in retrieval QA is the closest analogue of the crutch control and is absent from agent memory work. On the in-context side, the program's archived ideas decorative_retriever (retrieval-set overlap decides whether a bank can be frozen) and memory_dropout_coadaptation (bank swap for prompt optimizers coupled to self-editing memory) use related diagnostics on prompts, not weights.
Abstract: A growing family of agents is trained with a memory bank in the loop and then credited with 'learning to use memory'. Every such report compares against training without the memory, which changes the training data, or against an untrained model without the memory, which changes both. We hold the training trajectories fixed and vary only whether the retrieved block is present during training and at inference, producing a train-by-infer 2x2 on the same backbone and the same LoRA budget, then extend the inference axis with a disjoint equally-good bank (swap), a relevance-matched decoy bank, and no bank. Four contrasts fall out: content absorbed (trained-without-memory, no bank, versus base); untrained read benefit (base with bank versus base without); learned read skill (the interaction term); and bank co-adaptation (own bank versus swapped bank, trained versus untrained). We pre-register that the read-skill interaction is equivalent to zero within 3 points, that the memory-trained model stripped of memory falls at least 3 points below the memory-stripped-trained model on the same trajectories (crutch), and that its own-bank-minus-swapped-bank drop exceeds the untrained model's. Action-copy logging separates selective from indiscriminate reading. A secondary arm repeats the design with a short GRPO stage with and without a memory tool at matched rollout budget, and a cross-backbone cell tests whether the untrained read benefit of a bank is backbone-agnostic. The outcome tells the field whether 'trained to use memory' is content, crutch, or skill, on 7B-8B open models in days on one node.
Experiments: Backbones: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct primary, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct secondary (the cross-backbone cell uses the bank built by one on the other, untrained). Data: task-type-stratified split of the 1,465 local ALFWorld tasks into train-A (~500), train-B (~500) and held-out (~465), plus the 134 unseen-scene tasks; the base agent collects successful trajectories on train-A and train-B with up to three attempts; bank A and bank B are built from the respective successes and matched on size, task-type mix and mean trajectory length; decoy bank D pairs each query with relevance-matched trajectories from a different task type (same length distribution). Training arms, identical trajectories from train-A, identical LoRA (rank 32), steps and optimizer: T_M, SFT on prompts containing k=3 items retrieved from bank A under leave-one-task-out (the trajectory of the same task is never retrievable, which otherwise makes copying the trivial optimum); T_0, SFT on the same trajectories with the retrieved block deleted from the prompt; T_mix, 50% of examples with and 50% without the block (the RAFT-style control). Inference conditions for each of Base, T_0, T_M, T_mix: no bank; bank A at k=3; bank B at k=3 (swap); decoy D at k=3; and k=7 from bank A (dose ablation). Evaluation: 465 held-out x 5 seeds and 134 unseen-scene x 5 seeds, paired by task and seed across all cells. Decomposition (all paired with bootstrap CIs): content = T_0(none) - Base(none); untrained read = Base(A) - Base(none); read skill = [T_M(A) - T_M(none)] - [Base(A) - Base(none)]; crutch = T_0(none) - T_M(none); co-adaptation = [T_M(A) - T_M(B)] - [Base(A) - Base(B)]; decoy sensitivity = [T_M(D) - T_M(none)] - [Base(D) - Base(none)]. Reading probe: per episode, fraction of actions that are 4-gram copies of the retrieved items, split by whether the retrieved item is same-task-type (relevant) or decoy; a learned read skill predicts higher copying from relevant and lower from decoy items in T_M than in Base; a crutch predicts higher copying from both. Secondary RL arm (budget permitting): 300 GRPO steps from T_0 with and without a retrieve tool at matched rollout count, evaluated in the same inference grid, giving the memory-tool-RL version of the crutch and read-skill contrasts. Cross-backbone cell: bank A (built by Qwen) given to untrained Llama and vice versa, to report whether the untrained read benefit is content-general (G28).
Baselines and Ablations: Baselines: Base(none), Base(A) (the training-free memory baseline), T_0(none) (the plain SFT baseline of 2603.18272), T_M(A) (the retrieval-aware fine-tuning cell). Ablations: leave-one-task-out versus same-task retrieval allowed in training (shows the copying degenerate case and its crutch magnitude); T_mix as the RAFT-style fix; k=1 and k=7 at inference; retrieval by oracle task type versus embedding similarity; LoRA rank 16/64; trajectory count halved; success-only versus success-plus-failure banks; second backbone; the GRPO arm with and without the memory tool.
Falsifiable Predictions: P1 (read skill is null): the interaction term is inside a +/-3 point equivalence margin (TOST) on both held-out sets; rejected if the interaction's 95% CI excludes zero and exceeds 3 points, which would mean training with memory in context teaches a transferable reading behavior. P2 (crutch): T_M(none) is at least 3 points below T_0(none), paired; rejected if T_M(none) >= T_0(none) - noise, which would support the MemHarness-style claim that memory in the loop improves intrinsic capability. P3 (co-adaptation): T_M's own-bank-minus-swapped-bank drop exceeds Base's by at least 3 points; rejected if the two drops are equivalent, meaning the trained model reads a bank as generically as an untrained one. P4 (indiscriminate reading): T_M copies more actions from decoy items than Base does (ratio of decoy-copy rates >1.5) and its decoy penalty exceeds Base's; rejected if T_M copies less from decoys than Base. P5 (fix): T_mix closes at least half of the crutch gap while keeping at least 80% of T_M(A)'s gain. P6 (cross-backbone, descriptive): the untrained read benefit of a bank built by the other backbone is at least 60% of the own-bank benefit.
Measurement and Noise Control: Every contrast is a paired difference over the same tasks and seeds; 465 x 5 seeds gives an expected minimum detectable paired difference of about 3-4 points at 80% power, computed at pre-registration from the Base(none) run; predicted nulls (P1) use equivalence testing with the stated margin. Noise floor: two independently seeded training runs each of T_0 and T_M serve as null replicates, so any train-arm contrast must exceed the between-seed band; for the inference axis, one cell is re-scored twice. Bank A and bank B quality is verified before any training by evaluating Base(A) versus Base(B) on the held-out set, which must be equivalent within 2 points, otherwise banks are re-sampled; this check is pre-registered as Gate 0. Leave-one-task-out retrieval in training and the reading probe are logged per episode so that any crutch effect can be traced to copying rather than asserted. All thresholds and the amendment log are filed before the first confirmatory run.
